r: The applied work is real-time visual-gestural communication: producing and receiving signs, holding basic ASL conversations, parsing the grammar of a spatial language, and orienting to Deaf culture. These map to O*NET activities like Communicating with Persons Outside the Organization and Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships, executed in an embodied face-to-face modality. Task-exposure research ranks translators and interpreters near the top of exposure tables, which pressures foreign-language study when the task is text translation, but sign-language recognition and avatar generation lag spoken-language machine translation badly, and the course's aim is the student's own embodied communicative competence, not translation. As the base of the ASL sequence it is prerequisite scaffolding. At 24 months the instrumental need to acquire hands-on signing fluency is not eroded; the tools translate text, they do not sign for the learner.

By 2031, machine translation for spoken languages will be excellent and ubiquitous, and even signing-avatar systems will improve. That erodes the translation rationale, a genuine downward pressure the rating registers. What survives is the embodied core: conversing in a visual-gestural language in real time with Deaf interlocutors is a physical, interpersonal act that task-exposure frameworks place among the least automatable, and that no model performs on the learner's behalf. Sign-language AI adoption remains materially behind spoken-language tools, so realized automatability of the actual signing task stays limited. As foundational scaffolding for ASL II and III, the course's role holds across a catalog cycle. The rating stays Low, more protected than a spoken-language course because embodiment does heavier work here than transferable text translation. The main uncertainty is the pace of signing-recognition adoption.

A decade out, translation between English and signed languages may finally approach the fluency spoken-language tools reach sooner, and interpreting-as-task becomes substantially more automatable, lifting base automatability. Even so, the specific competence this course builds, a human able to sign and read signs in live, culturally-situated interaction, is embodied and interpersonal, and embodiment keeps the rating from rising to High. The most plausible 2036 change is that AI mediates more Deaf-hearing exchanges, not that a beginning student stops needing to physically acquire the language. Foundational scaffolding for the sequence persists in the central case. I rate Medium, with genuine uncertainty: if signing-avatar and recognition systems mature faster than expected, erosion could be sharper; if embodiment and cultural-fit concerns slow adoption, weaker. No confident point prediction.

ASL 1020.d: This course is a continuation of ASL 1010 emphasizing expressive language as well as increasing competence with receptive language skills. The course continues to build vocabulary and familiarity with the complex grammar (morphology and syntax) of this visual language. The deaf experience and culture is integrated throughout.

ASL 1021.d: This one-credit course complements the existing ASL 1020 - American Sign Language II or its equivalent. It adds a professional dimension to the study of American Sign Language, with two main objectives: enhancing students' ability to communicate in specific, career-relevant situations in ASL, and developing intercultural expertise for effective communication with individuals from diverse cultural backgrounds.

ASL 1030.d: In this course, students continue to build their foundation of signing skills and knowledge acquired in American Sign Language (ASL) I and II. Students learn more vocabulary signs and more complex grammatical features using classifiers through narratives and dialogues. In addition to improving their signing skills, students learn more about Deaf culture in class and from reading assignments. Learning about Deaf culture helps students understand the particular cultural norms, behaviors, and formative shared experiences distinct to those who approach the world from a visual perspective and use ASL.

r: Unlike the signing courses, this is a study-and-analysis course requiring no ASL: students examine the history, social dynamics, values, traditions, and contemporary experience of the Deaf community, plus ASL's role and the impact of societal attitudes and technology. The applied tasks, explaining Deaf history and culture, analyzing social dynamics, producing cultural-competence writing through discussion and readings, map to O*NET's Getting Information and Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others, and are largely digital-deliverable rather than embodied. Task-exposure research classifies this kind of factual-explanatory humanities content as exposed, and observed-usage data shows writing and information tasks prominent in AI use. Crucially, the course carries no GT-Pathways designation in the record, so no transfer mandate caps exposure. At 24 months the instrumental case already registers Medium: AI competently explains Deaf culture, though the course's cultural-competence aim retains value.

By 2031, AI will fluently deliver, tutor, and analyze Deaf-culture content, history, social dynamics, cultural norms, and generate cultural-competence writing on demand, substantially eroding the information-and-analysis rationale that is this course's core applied work. Unlike the catalog's appreciation courses in music or dance, no GT-Pathways designation locks this course into the general-education transfer core, so the exposure that elsewhere is capped at Medium is not capped here. The residual human value, genuine embodied cultural competence in relating to Deaf individuals, is real but is not the graded analytical work the course centers on. The rating rises to High. The hedge: if the course functions in practice as a transfer or interpreting-program requirement not captured in this record, institutional lock would pull it down; on the description alone, exposure runs high.

A decade out, AI will be an authoritative, interactive explainer of Deaf history, culture, and social dynamics, and the analytical and writing tasks this course builds are among the more automatable in the catalog once no transfer mandate caps them. The durable residue is embodied cultural competence enacted in relationship with Deaf people, but that is interpersonal practice the course studies rather than the declarative-knowledge work it assesses. I rate High, the clearest case in this batch of AI performing the applied task, while flagging real uncertainty: this rating turns heavily on the absent GT-Pathways designation, and if the course carries a social-sciences or humanities mandate not shown here, the central case would cap at Medium. No confident point prediction, but the direction is upward.
ASL 2100.d: Through this course students will acquire comprehensive understanding of the vibrant culture of the Deaf community. Through exploring the history, social dynamics, values, and traditions of Deaf culture, students gain insights into the unique experiences and perspectives of Deaf individuals. The course also covers the significance of American Sign Language (ASL) and its role within the community, as well as the impact of societal attitudes and technological advancements on Deaf people's lives. Students engage in discussions, readings, and activities that promote cultural competence and respect for Deaf culture. No prior knowledge of ASL is required for this course. Anthropology
